rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration are defined as limits: $v = dx/dt$ and $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$. Graphically, $v$ is the tangent slope of the $x$–$t$ curve and $a$ the tangent slope of the $v$–$t$ curve, while areas under $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ curves give displacement and velocity change.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Instantaneous velocity: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$
Instantaneous acceleration: $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$
Displacement from velocity: $x_2 - x_1 = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v\,dt$ (area under $v$–$t$ curve)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Limit Definition Universality:** Instantaneous velocity $v = dx/dt$ and acceleration $a = dv/dt$ are defined as limits ($\Delta t o 0$). They apply to *any* motion — uniform or non-uniform, constant or variable acceleration. The SUVAT equations ($v = u + at$, etc.) are special cases valid *only* for constant $a$.  ·  **Graph Duality — Slopes vs Areas:** On $x$-$t$ graph: slope of tangent = $v$. On $v$-$t$ graph: slope of tangent = $a$; area under curve = displacement. On $a$-$t$ graph: area under curve = change in velocity. Mixing up slope/area is the most common graph error.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: Carry units through calculus: if $x$ is in metres and $t$ in seconds, $v$ is m/s and $a$ is m/s² automatically.  ·  Note 2: NEB graph questions award marks for BOTH slope reasoning and area reasoning — label which you used.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Example 1: $x(t) = 3t^2$ m → $v = 6t$ m/s; at $t = 2$ s the instantaneous velocity is 12 m/s, while the average velocity over 0–2 s is $\frac{12-0}{2} = 6$ m/s — different because the motion speeds up.  ·  Example 2: A metro train's $v$–$t$ graph: trapezoid of acceleration, cruise, braking. Displacement = area of trapezoid; acceleration = slope in each segment.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Instantaneous velocity equals average velocity.' ✅ Only when motion is uniform. In general $v_{inst} = dx/dt$ while $v_{avg} = \Delta x/\Delta t$; they coincide only if the $x$–$t$ graph is a straight line.  ·  ❌ 'Negative acceleration always means slowing down.' ✅ Slowing means $v$ and $a$ have OPPOSITE signs. A ball thrown upward (up = positive) has $v > 0$ with $a = -g$ — it slows going up and speeds up coming down, with the SAME downward acceleration throughout.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Differentiate five polynomial position functions, evaluating $v$ and $a$ at specified instants.  ·  Task 2: Sketch $x$–$t$, $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ triplet graphs for: uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion, and simple back-and-forth motion.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: 'At rest' ⇒ set $dx/dt = 0$ and solve for $t$; then check the sign of $v$ on both sides to classify pause vs reversal.  ·  Trick 2: In graph MCQs, remember: slope of $x$–$t$ = $v$; slope of $v$–$t$ = $a$; area of $v$–$t$ = $x$; area of $a$–$t$ = $v$.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q2. Distinguish between average acceleration and instantaneous acceleration with one example each.  ·  Q3. For $x(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t$ (m), find when the velocity is zero and classify each instant (pause vs reversal).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 1: NEB regularly sets 2-3 mark calculus questions: differentiate $x(t)$, evaluate $v$ and $a$ at a given time — show the derivative step explicitly.  ·  Exam Tip 2: In graph-conversion questions (given $v$–$t$, sketch $x$–$t$), track curvature: constant $v$ → straight $x$ line; linear $v$ → parabolic $x$.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concept 1: Limit definition — instantaneous quantities are average quantities over a vanishing interval.  ·  Concept 2: Derivative chain: $x \xrightarrow{d/dt} v \xrightarrow{d/dt} a$; integrals run the reverse way with initial conditions.  ·  Concept 3: Graph duality — slopes give rates (v, a); areas give accumulations (x, v).  ·  Concept 4: Sign logic — direction of motion from sign of $v$; speeding up/slowing down from relative signs of $v$ and $a$.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent of the $x$–$t$ graph; instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the $v$–$t$ graph.  ·  Displacement is the area under the $v$–$t$ graph; change in velocity is the area under the $a$–$t$ graph.  ·  $v = 0$ does not imply $a = 0$ — turning points have zero velocity but non-zero acceleration.  ·  Speeding up ⟺ $v$ and $a$ share the same sign; slowing down ⟺ opposite signs.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Calculus was invented (Newton and Leibniz, 1660s–70s) precisely to handle instantaneous quantities — physics and calculus were born together, and Newton's name for the derivative was the 'fluxion'.  ·  Car speedometers show instantaneous speed, while trip computers computing distance ÷ time show average speed — the two can differ enormously in city traffic.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q4. Sketch the $v$–$t$ graph for a ball thrown vertically upward and returning; mark where $v = 0$ and the sign of $a$ throughout.  ·  Q5. A particle moves with $v = kt$ where $k = 2$ m/s². Find its instantaneous acceleration and displacement after 3 s from rest.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Exam Tip 3: When asked 'when is the particle at rest', also state the acceleration at that instant — examiners expect the follow-through.  ·  Exam Tip 4: Define the limit properly in theory questions: shrinking interval, ratio of small changes — vague wording loses marks.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Example 3: $v(t) = 8 - 4t$: the particle reverses at $t = 2$ s where $v = 0$ but $a = -4$ m/s² throughout — illustrating reversal with constant acceleration.  ·  Example 4: Two instants with equal speeds but different velocities: $v = +10$ m/s at $t_1$ and $v = -10$ m/s at $t_2$ — same speed, opposite direction of motion.

rows.text: The instantaneous velocity of a particle is given by: → B  ·  If x(t) = 5t² m, the instantaneous velocity at t = 3 s is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version complements the original note with the limit-definition approach, calculus forms and graphical slope reasoning for instantaneous velocity and acceleration.  ·  **Average quantities first:** average velocity $v_{avg} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ uses the whole interval; average acceleration $a_{avg} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ likewise. They smooth out everything that happened in between — a car doing 100 km in 2 h has $v_{avg} = 50$ km/h regardless of traffic.  ·  **The limit idea:** instantaneous velocity is the average velocity as $\Delta t \to 0$: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$. It answers 'how fast RIGHT NOW' — exactly what a speedometer reads.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Generality — the derivative definitions hold for any acceleration; constant-$a$ equations are a special case.  ·  Definition and significance of Instantaneous Velocity & Instantaneous Acceleration.  ·  Velocity from acceleration: $v_2 - v_1 = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} a\,dt$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Rest condition: $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0$; reversal check: sign change of $v$ around that instant  ·  **Sign Logic for Speeding/Slowing:** Speeding up $\Leftrightarrow$ $v$ and $a$ have *same* sign. Slowing down $\Leftrightarrow$ $v$ and $a$ have *opposite* signs. This is true regardless of coordinate choice. At a turning point ($v=0$), $a eq 0$ (e.g., ball at top of flight: $v=0$, $a=g$).  ·  Derivatives go down the chain $x \to v \to a$; integrals go up $a \to v \to x$, using initial conditions.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The limit definition is valid for ANY motion — SUVAT equations are special cases of constant acceleration only.  ·  Connection of Instantaneous Velocity & Instantaneous Acceleration to other topics  ·  ❌ 'The area under an $x$–$t$ graph gives velocity.' ✅ The SLOPE of $x$–$t$ gives velocity; the AREA under a $v$–$t$ graph gives displacement. Mixing these up is the classic graph-question error.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'At the turning point, acceleration is zero.' ✅ At a reversal, $v = 0$ but $a$ is NOT zero (e.g. a ball at the top of its flight has $v = 0$, $a = g$ downward). Zero velocity ≠ zero acceleration.  ·  ❌ 'Speed can be negative.' ✅ Speed is $|v|$, always non-negative; velocity carries the sign (direction).  ·  ❌ 'If $v = 0$ at an instant, the particle has stopped permanently.' ✅ $v = 0$ can be a momentary pause (top of a throw) — check the acceleration to know what happens next.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Example 5: From $a = 6t$ and $v(0) = 2$ m/s: integrate to $v = 3t^2 + 2$ and, with $x(0) = 0$, $x = t^3 + 2t$ — showing how derivatives run downward ($x \to v \to a$) and integrals run upward.  ·  Note 3: When integrating acceleration, always determine integration constants from given initial conditions.  ·  Note 4: In 'is the particle speeding up?' questions, compare signs of $v$ and $a$ at that instant — not the sign of $a$ alone.
